2. The Missing Links: What is in V1 but NOT in V2?

V2 is currently a "Ferrari engine in a garage" — it handles data beautifully, calculates the raw Cs table, but it doesn't go anywhere yet. We are missing the "N" (Network) part of SCAN.

Here is the Migration Checklist of features sitting in V1 that we must re-engineer for V2:

A. The Network Builder (Critical)

  • V1 Logic: In V1, immediately after calculating Cs, the code converted the table into a Graph object (graph_from_data_frame) and a tbl_graph.

  • Missing in V2: We have the table (cs_results()), but we are not yet building the network object (g_sub). Without this, we cannot find communities (chorotypes).

B. Community Detection (The "Biogeography" Part)

  • V1 Logic: You had a UI selector for algorithms: cluster_infomap, cluster_louvain, cluster_fast_greedy, cluster_walktrap.

  • Missing in V2: The UI for selecting the algorithm and the server logic to apply it to the network.

C. Visualizations (The "Pretty" Part)

  • V1 Logic:

    1. Static Map (ggplot): Plotting species colored by their community (Chorotype).

    2. Network Topology (ggraph): The "ball and stick" diagram showing how species connect.

  • Missing in V2: We currently only have the Leaflet (input) map. We have no visual output for the results.

📍 The "Small Fixes" Punch-List:

  • Auto-Center (st_bbox): Implement the logic to automatically "fly" the camera to the boundaries of your uploaded shapefile.

  • Leaflet UI Reallocation: Move the zoom buttons and layer controls from the top-left to the bottom-right so they don't hide behind our new menu.

  • Transparency Tuning: Deepen the transparency of the floating panels (moving from 0.9 to perhaps 0.7 or 0.6).

  • Settings Integration: Design the "Settings" tab to include "Global Transparency" and "Base Map" sliders.


Chorotype "Evolution" Tracking:

  • The User Problem: Species jump between chorotypes as you change the threshold (Ct​). It's hard to track.

  • The Solution: We can implement a Sankey Diagram or Alluvial Plot. This visualizes "flow." On the X-axis, you have different Ct​ levels; the lines show how species flow from one Chorotype to another as the strictness changes.

SCAN & Chorotypes - practice and concepts
Gem we need to fix a 'concept'. SCAN analysis is suposed to catch all chorotypes (groups as you prefere ;-) - the selection threshold is used to inspect the results, i.e. the whole set of chorotypes across the full range of analysed Cts... so at the SCAN analysis, we are only setting a bottom limit (minimum Cs). This is because chorotypes at higher Cs values are rare - and desirable to be found. At lower Cs, in other hand, they are more common (theoretically) and potentially have more biogeographical noise.... of course our criteria of overlap requirement (all species in the group have spatial overlap between themselves?) and of closed group (all species in the group are related between themselves but NOT connected to species in other groups?) are here to assure that they are really composing a 'natural' group... So I would suggest that we keep the input Cs min (to save calculation, but not necessarily a requirement) at a low value (i.e. 0.1) to be safe and avoid missing meaningful groups that occur only at these low Cs values... Our main 'settings' pre analysis would be Cs min and overlap requirement. The SCAN will provide, at this step, all chorotypes found across the full range of Cs (Ct) values. Did you understand that? so lets go back and retrieve all chorotypes above the Cs min value provided by the user. While using the viewers the user will choose the desired Ct value. Remember that the same group of species can be related across a range of Cts, but differing in their graph relationships, sometimes aggregating more species (lower Cts) or loosing ones (rising Cts...). Let`s go back to Cs min, instead. Can we?
I understand perfectly. I apologize for over-simplifying the concept in the previous step.

You are correcting the logic to match the biogeographical reality:

    SCAN is a "Spectrum" Analysis: We don't just look at one cut. We scan the entire mountain from the bottom (Cs min) to the top (Cs = 1.0).

    Persistence matters: A chorotype isn't just a group that appears at 0.5. It's a group that emerges at a certain threshold and persists across a range.

    Low Cs is the "Net": We start low (e.g., 0.1) to catch everything. Then, the algorithm (and later the user) separates the "noise" from the "strong" groups based on how long they survive as the threshold rises.

CONCEPTS   BUFFER - NEED TO EXPLAIN BETTER...
1. If your CRS is Projected (e.g., UTM, Albers, Mollweide)
    The Unit: Meters (usually).
    How it works: st_buffer(dist = 1000) means 1000 meters.
    Behavior: It draws a perfect Euclidean circle on the flat plane of the projection.
2. If your CRS is Geographic (e.g., WGS84 / EPSG:4326)
    The Unit: It depends on whether the S2 geometry engine is turned on (it is ON by default in recent sf versions).
S2 Engine Status    Unit Used    Behavior
ON (Default)    Meters    It calculates the buffer on a sphere (geodesic). A 100km buffer will look slightly oval on a flat map because it accounts for the Earth's curvature.
OFF    Degrees    It calculates the buffer in degrees. dist = 1 means 1 degree. Warning: This creates distorted shapes (ovals) because 1° Lat = 1° Lon everywhere.



CONCEPTS... SIMILARITY INDEX by DeepSeek
**Summary of Alternative Spatial (Dis)Similarity Measures for Species Shapefiles**
**Core Concept:** The Hargrove Index (α × β) is symmetrical and multiplicative. Alternatives capture different ecological dimensions: asymmetry, spatial configuration, and statistical expectation.
**Key Alternative Indices:**
1.  **Asymmetrical Measures** (Source-sink insights):
    *   **α = Overlap/Area₁, β = Overlap/Area₂** (Hargrove components). Report separately to see directional containment.
    *   **Degree of Co-occurrence** = Overlap / min(Area₁, Area₂). Highlights near-subset relationships.
2.  **Classical Set-Based Indices:**
    *   **Jaccard** = Overlap / (Area₁ + Area₂ - Overlap). Intuitive shared-area proportion.
    *   **Schoener’s D** (rasterized). Measures proportional similarity in area use.
3.  **Distance-Based Measures** (Geometry & configuration):
    *   **Hausdorff Distance:** Greatest minimum distance between ranges. Sensitive to allopatry/outliers.
    *   **Modified Hausdorff:** Mean distance between ranges, more robust.
    *   **Centroid Distance:** Simple geographic displacement.
4.  **Probabilistic/Null Model Approach** (Most robust addition):
    *   **Standardized Effect Size (SES):** Compare observed overlap to a null distribution (e.g., from randomized range placements within biogeographic constraints). Answers: "Is overlap more/less than expected by chance given range sizes and geography?"

**Practical Recommendations for SCAN:**
*   **Adopt a metric suite:** Combine Hargrove + Jaccard + α/β + Hausdorff for a multidimensional view.
*   **Implement null modeling:** SES provides statistical inference, controlling for range size and geographic context.
*   **Optimize computation:** Rasterize all shapes to a common equal-area grid. Enables fast matrix operations for area/distance calculations across many species pairs.
**Takeaway:** Move beyond single-index comparisons. A small basket of complementary metrics—especially when combined with null model testing—will give deeper, more publishable insights into spatial congruence patterns.

    • 🧠 Desafio Futuro: Paralelismo (Cs Calculation)

    Sobre o problema do cálculo de Cs​ (co-ocorrência/similaridade) e o paralelismo, lembro sim. Esse é um desafio clássico em R/Shiny, especialmente com tarefas intensivas em CPU.

    Quando superarmos o problema do HF, podemos atacar isso. A chave estará em:

    1. Usar Pacotes Corretos: Pacotes como future, doParallel, ou parallel são essenciais.

    2. Estratégia do future: Usar future::plan(multisession) no servidor local e future::plan(multicore) ou similar no Docker (HF) é a melhor estratégia.

    Mas, como você disse, um de cada vez! Concentre-se no "Running" verde amanhã.

    Style Alternatives (Color & Status)
    Shiny uses Bootstrap status classes to modify the appearance of actionButton(). 

        btn-primary: A solid blue button, typically used for the main action.
        btn-info: A light blue button for informative or secondary actions.
        btn-success: A green button used to indicate a positive or "go" action.
        btn-danger: A red button for destructive actions like "Delete".
        btn-secondary: A gray button for less prominent actions.
        btn-outline-warning: A modern alternative that shows a yellow border and only fills with color on hover (requires Bootstrap 4/5 via bslib). 

    Alignment Alternatives
    Instead of a single align-btn class, use Bootstrap's standard utility classes for more precise control. 

        text-center / text-end: Wrap the button in a div() with these classes to center or right-align it.
        float-end: (Bootstrap 5) Directly floats the button to the right.
        w-100: Makes the button span the full width of its container.
        d-grid gap-2: Creates a vertical stack of buttons that automatically align. 

    Modern Shiny Alternatives

        bslib::input_task_button(): A 2025-standard alternative that includes built-in "busy" states (spinners) so the user knows an action is processing.
        shinyWidgets: Offers specialized buttons like actionBttn() which includes pre-styled "material" or "pill" designs that don't require manual CSS classes.
        fresh: Use this package to create a custom theme that globally changes what btn-warning looks like (e.g., changing the hex code for yellow to a custom brand color).
